title: Does bracket order change the bill?
hook: Same three matrices, same answer. Same cost?

doesNotKnow: that the same product costs 6 times more in a different bracketing

misconception: Multiplying matrices costs the same whichever pair you multiply first.
objective: The learner can explain that the bracketing of a matrix chain changes the size of the middle product and so the cost: for 10x30, 30x5, 5x60, (AB)C costs 4,500 multiplications and A(BC) 27,000, six times as much, for the same 10x60 result.

claims.text: Multiplying a p×q matrix by a q×r matrix the usual way costs p·q·r single multiplications (question and stage rule line).
claims.source: CLRS 4e section 14.2 (matrix-chain multiplication): computing a p x q by q x r product with the standard algorithm takes pqr scalar multiplications. Also CLRS 3e section 15.2. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Derivation: each of the p x r entries is a length-q dot product, q multiplications; own triple-loop count for 10x30 by 30x5 = 1,500. CLRS 4e 14.2 / 3e 15.2 attribution consistent with my knowledge; book not opened, the claim does not depend on it.

Demo.tsx mul() computes each step's cost with the p*q*r rule the stage prints (TOP, BOT, RATIO). Builder's node script (2026-10-14) re-ran it: 1500 + 3000 and 9000 + 18000. The sizes are the brief's own (CLRS's own three-matrix example uses different sizes, 10x100, 100x5, 5x50, from memory: check before relying on it). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Arithmetic re-run: 1,500 + 3,000 = 4,500; 9,000 + 18,000 = 27,000; ratio 6. Own DP gives 4,500 as the optimum for dims [10,30,5,60]. Builder's recalled CLRS example (10x100, 100x5, 5x50) also matches my knowledge (7,500 vs 75,000); not learner-visible.

claims.text: Both orders give the same 10×60 matrix (stage '✓ same 10×60 as above'; reveal 'every bracketing gives the same matrix').
claims.source: Matrix multiplication is associative: ((AB)C)_ij = sum_k sum_l A_il B_lk C_kj = (A(BC))_ij. Result size is rows of A by columns of C, 10 x 60. CLRS 4e section 14.2 notes the product is the same for every parenthesization. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Associativity derivation as given; result rows of A by columns of C = 10 x 60. Stage '✓ same 10×60 as above' only after both orders run.

claims.text: The 30×5 by 5×60 step alone costs 9,000, twice the whole (AB)C bill.
claims.source: Arithmetic from c2: 9,000 = 2 x 4,500. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: 9,000 = 2 x 4,500.

claims.text: For a longer chain, trying every split point of every sub-chain, shortest sub-chains first, finds the cheapest order.
claims.source: CLRS 4e section 14.2: optimal substructure over split points k and the bottom-up MATRIX-CHAIN-ORDER, which fills the table by increasing chain length (O(n^3) time). 3e section 15.2. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: The method is right but the wording is not: 'cheapest sub-chains first' reads as processing sub-chains in order of cost. MATRIX-CHAIN-ORDER (CLRS 4e 14.2, recalled, not opened) solves sub-chains in order of length, shortest first. Own check: bottom-up by length equals brute force over all bracketings on 2,000 random chains (fc21/mc.mjs). Fix (builder): 'shortest sub-chains first' in Demo.tsx reveal and claim text. · Builder 2026-10-14 (W-196): reworded per pass 21; awaiting re-check. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Reveal text matches. Re-derived optimal substructure (cost = left + right + p(i-1)p(k)p(j)); own bottom-up-by-length DP equals brute force over all bracketings on 2,000 chains of 2-7 matrices. CLRS not opened; not relied on.

recall.question: You must multiply three matrices of sizes 2x50, 50x2 and 2x50. Which order should you multiply first?
options: The first two, because the middle result is only 2x2
The last two, because the middle result is only 2x2
It does not matter: the answer is the same matrix
recall.why: The first pair makes a 2x2 box for 2·50·2 = 200, then 2·2·50 = 200: 400 in all. The last pair makes a 50x50 box for 50·2·50 = 5,000, then 2·50·50 = 5,000 more. Same answer, 25 times the price.
